title: The strange rules of the dinner table
text: Table manners look like {{1}} rules invented purely to torment children, yet they have a history and a purpose. For most of the past, diners ate from a {{2}} pot, armed with fingers or a shared knife. The individual plate is a surprisingly {{3}} invention, and the fork met furious {{4}} when it arrived in Renaissance Italy: one Venetian noblewoman was denounced by a cleric for {{5}} her food with such excessive delicacy that she was judged to insult nature itself. Etiquette, in other words, has always been social technology — devices for keeping the peace among people crowded around food. The details vary astonishingly: in Japan, the slurp {{6}} appreciation, while in much of Europe it appals; the left hand eats politely in one country and offends in another. Yet beneath the variations, all these codes {{7}} the same function: they turn hungry strangers into a temporary society, spare table-partners from one another's germs, and mark the moment when eating becomes a shared ceremony. Good manners, in the end, are simply {{8}} in disguise — a slow, repetitive way of saying that you are safe among us.

gaps.explanation: 'ate from a shared pot' — passive participle.
'a surprisingly late invention' — arriving recently in time.
'met furious resistance' — people pushed back against it.
'for eating her food with delicacy' — gerund after a preposition.
'the slurp signals appreciation' — verb needed; nouns fail here.
'codes perform the same function' — do the job they exist for.
'simply hospitality in disguise' — the friendly welcome of a guest.
